title: Public art, culture and parks plans advance
subtitle: Emergency management by-law, community grant changes, City Hall clock relocation study and seniors' concerns about the parks plan
overview: The committee spent most of the afternoon on three long-range plans from Public Services: a revised Public Art Policy, the first Culture Plan 2030, and the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. It recommended all three for Council's approval. Costs for each were referred to future budget processes, so the pace of delivery will depend on the 2024-2027 multi-year budget.

The committee also recommended a new Emergency Management Response By-law and dissolving the Community Grant Allocation Panel, with grant awards delegated to the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer of Public Services. On the Public Art Policy, it recommended that staff study the possible future relocation of the City Hall clock for the 2027 bicentennial. The City Hall bell, recently installed in the City Hall courtyard, was removed from that direction {{vote:m8}}.

Earlier, a closed session on the Clair-Maltby Secondary Plan and Ontario Land Tribunal matter ended with Council receiving information and giving direction to staff. No further detail was made public. Because the committee's decisions are recommendations, Council will take them up later this month. Several councillors said they would follow up with staff on details before then.

decisions.detail: The committee directed staff to bring forward a by-law repealing the 2019 Emergency Management Response By-law and replacing it with an updated one.

The committee recommended dissolving the Community Grant Allocation Panel, delegating grant awards to the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer of Public Services, and adding equity-related policy changes.
The committee recommended approving the updated policy, widening the Public Art Reserve Fund's sources of funds, and referring the costs to the multi-year budget process.
The committee recommended referring the potential future relocation of the City Hall clock to staff and the advisory committees for costing and consideration in the 2027 commemorations.
The committee recommended approving Culture Plan 2030 and referring its implementation costs to the 2024-2027 multi-year budget process.
The committee recommended approving the August 2023 plan and referring its funding needs to future operating and capital budgets.

debate: On the Public Art Policy, one councillor proposed adding a commitment to apply the Community Engagement Framework early in identifying public art opportunities. Staff said they had not had time to assess the staffing, cost and timing effects and that the framework already guides city work. The motion was withdrawn so staff could prepare a memo.

On the City Hall bell and clock, a mover said the bell's current courtyard location is not publicly accessible and was chosen without public consultation. Others argued that moving the bell was a low priority given budget pressures. Staff noted that the bell is anchored in the foundation, so moving it would be costly, and that the clock was dismantled long ago and may not be restorable. Staff also said the bicentennial budget could not cover a bell relocation.

On Culture Plan 2030, delegates described a shortage of affordable rehearsal, studio and performance space. They also described artists leaving the city, and said culture's value is not only financial. One councillor questioned the plan's specific call to advocate for basic income for artists, citing the city's broader advocacy priorities. Staff offered to discuss it before Council meets.

On the Parks and Recreation Master Plan, a delegate from the seniors' association asked for changes to the older adult recommendations and for printed program guides. Staff said the plan already covers these items and that they would continue partnering with the association. Councillors also raised shade, accessible playground surfaces, water access for community gardens, and the loss of park space to stormwater infrastructure.
